1:
Henry makes the terror a matter of who had held out longest. The people's hearts had fainted already, as Rahab had told the spies; the kings had kept their spirits up, promising themselves that with their country populous and their cities fortified they could hold against invaders. What broke them was not the crossing but the manner of it, that Israel came over by a miracle with the God of nature manifestly fighting for them. Calvin looks at what the fear did and did not produce. It left them destitute of counsel and strength, but it did not incline their minds to seek a remedy; they remained as hard-hearted as before, so that the dread which ought to have urged them to caution only hurried them on headlong. He adds why it was sent: not for their sake but for Israel's, so that the enemy was already routed before the conflict began. Wesley supplies the local reason they had grown careless, that Jordan was their bulwark and the Israelites had lingered in the neighbouring country without attacking, and he sees a providence in it, that Israel might quietly receive circumcision and the passover before the fighting started. Clarke, Gill and Ellicott agree that the Amorites and Canaanites here stand for the rest.

The timing of the command is where Henry does his best work. God ordered the circumcision at the very moment the country was in consternation, because only then could it be done safely in an enemy's land: their hearts being melted, their hands were tied, and they could not take the advantage against Israel that Simeon and Levi took against the Shechemites when those men were sore. Henry then presses the point that makes it a command rather than a stratagem. Joshua could not be sure the enemy would stay paralysed, so had he ordered a general circumcision of his own head he might justly have been censured as imprudent; the thing was good in itself but in the eye of reason unseasonable. Since God commanded it, he must not consult with flesh and blood. Gill and Keil both mark the same conjunction more briefly, that the dread which had seized the inhabitants made this a fit time for what was next ordered. Calvin turns instead on the long neglect that made it necessary, refusing the usual excuse that a people constantly under arms had no leisure. He calls the apology frivolous: the omission could have originated only in distrust, and the seal of the covenant was more precious than a hundred lives.

On the knives Clarke and Ellicott disagree about the Hebrew and about what follows from it. Clarke reads knives of rock or flint and asks why a people who plainly had iron should use stone. His answer is that metal was probably unlawful in the rite, and he assembles the parallels: Zipporah taking a sharp stone, the Egyptian refusal to use metal for incisions in preparing a body, the altar that must be built of unhewn stones lest a tool of iron pollute it, and the Ethiopian tribe that still circumcises with stone knives. He adds a physical reason as well, that a stone edge leaves no metal particles to oxidize in the wound, so it inflames less and heals sooner. Ellicott answers that the word in question denotes the edge of a tool rather than its material, so that keen-edged knives is the better translation, and he cites other places where it plainly means edge. He grants they may have been stone all the same, and supports it from an addition in the Greek at the end of the book, where the stone knives are buried with Joshua. On the second time both Keil and Wesley refuse to press the phrase into a repetition of one act upon the same people.
3:
Gill removes a difficulty the English hides. Joshua no more circumcised the people himself than he made the knives himself; he ordered both and saw them done. The rite was never restricted to any order of men, not to priests or Levites, so anyone might perform it, and a work that looks impossibly large could therefore be finished quickly. Wesley reaches the same conclusion from the calendar rather than the law: it had to be done fast because the passover was approaching, so many hands were necessarily used, and he thinks it probable that the Israelites who had settled beyond Jordan were circumcised at the same time, though the text does not say so. Keil supplies the detail that fixes the place, that the spot was afterwards called the hill of the foreskins because the foreskins were buried there.

On why the rite had lapsed for a generation the sources divide between an excuse and a judgment. Clarke takes it as a dispensation: owing to their unsettled state God appears to have set the obligation aside for the time being. Wesley offers that reading first, that either the parents or the rulers omitted it by divine permission, since the passover itself might be neglected on a journey, and then sets it aside for a harder answer. He prefers to see a continued token of God's displeasure for their unbelief and murmuring, a standing sign that they should never have the benefit of the very promise circumcision sealed. Ellicott approaches it from the phrase reproach of Egypt, which puzzles him because everyone born in Egypt had been circumcised. His solution is that the wandering years are a blank in the narrative, the chapters of Numbers belonging to them recording no progress in time or place, and that a people who had turned back in their hearts to Egypt omitted the sign of the covenant as though they were no longer God's.

What made this the moment is answered most fully by Clarke, and in terms that carry past the passage. Another passover was at hand, and no uncircumcised man could be reckoned within the covenant or keep the feast that sealed it; from that he draws the parallel that since baptism succeeded circumcision and the Lord's Supper succeeded the passover, no one in his own church is admitted to the one before receiving the other. Wesley lists the reasons together: a testimony that God was reconciled and would not further impute the parents' rebellion, the removal of the impediment of constant travel, preparation for the feast, distinction from the Canaanites whose land they had entered, and ratification of the covenant that promised them that land. Ellicott adds the turn on which his own reading depends, that the passage of Jordan was the practical proof of Israel's restoration to favour. He notes too that the first person used here suggests the whole passage from the previous chapter onward is meant as the fathers' reply to the children's question. Gill keeps the arithmetic honest, taking the forty years as a round number short by a few days.
8:
Clarke measures the risk before praising the obedience. He cites Chardin, who was told by renegadoes circumcised among the Mohammedans that adults kept their beds about three weeks and could walk only with great difficulty; and he asks how it was that the inhabitants of the land did not attack and destroy them, as might easily have been done, and as happened to the Shechemites. Joshua, he says, as an able general would have seen at once that the measure exposed his whole host to annihilation, and in the teeth of his enemies he nonetheless reduced the greater part of his army to total helplessness, trusting the arm of God. Clarke then asks the question that follows: why not order it while they were still safe east of Jordan? Because God chose to bring them into straits where no counsel or might but his own could save them, so that the excellence of the power might be seen to be his. Wesley says the same in a sentence, that it was an act of great faith to accept such pain and danger in a place where they were hemmed in between Jordan and their enemies. Gill notes only that the work seems to have been finished in a single day.

The reproach of Egypt divides them four ways. Clarke takes it as the reproach of uncircumcision itself, which had made them resemble the uncircumcised Egyptians, a people the Hebrews held to be in the grossest impurity; and he turns the point into an argument that Israel cannot have received the rite from Egypt, since they would not have thought abominable the very nation from whom they had the mark that made them pure. Wesley keeps the same general sense but offers three grounds for the name, that the neighbouring nations descended from Abraham by the concubines were circumcised while the Egyptians were not, that Israel coming out of Egypt was reckoned a sort of Egyptian, or that many had neglected the duty while in Egypt for worldly reasons. Keil reads the genitive the other way, as the reproach proceeding from Egypt, meaning the Egyptian taunt that Jehovah had brought the people out only to destroy them in the desert, which stood against Israel as long as it wandered and died there. Calvin rejects two readings as far fetched and settles on a political one: they were freed from the charge of being deserters and rebels, the renewal of the ancient covenant showing that their liberty was restored by God.

On the name of the place Clarke and Wesley agree that it means rolling or a rolling away, and Calvin uses it to dispose of a rival explanation. Some had taken the cut foreskin to be what was called Gilgal, because it made a kind of circle; Calvin answers that this abandons the literal meaning and has recourse to a very unnecessary fiction, since the place plainly took its name from the removal of the disgrace. Ellicott alone declines to argue the phrase at all and reaches instead for what it anticipates, setting beside it the promise that the Lord will swallow up death in victory and take away the rebuke of his people from off all the earth, the circumcision made without hands in the putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh, and the moment when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption. The effect is to read the rolling away at Gilgal as the first instance of something the prophets and the apostle carry further, rather than as a difficulty in the Hebrew to be settled.
10:
Henry sets the scene as a soldier's, observing that men taking the field think themselves excused from religious exercises, while Joshua opened his campaign with one act of devotion after another, and kept the feast in the plains of Jericho as if in defiance of the Canaanites round about. Ellicott counts it the third passover in Israel's history, two belonging to the going out and this one to the coming in. Whether it was the third because the others had lapsed is disputed. Henry, Wesley and Keil all take it that the ordinance had been suspended through the wilderness years, Wesley citing the prophet's question whether Israel offered sacrifices those forty years, and Henry treating the revival as God comforting them again after the time he had afflicted them. Calvin refuses this. It is not probable, he argues, that what God had lately ordered to be kept in all their generations should be cast aside within two years, nor credible that they would bury the memory of so recent a favour that quickly; and to the objection that the uncircumcised could not eat it he replies that they were dispensed from the law in this as in other parts of legal worship they certainly did continue. Clarke raises a different difficulty, that a people circumcised three days earlier could not naturally have been fit to keep it.

The corn they ate divides them over a word that occurs nowhere else. Gill and Wesley take it for last year's corn, Gill because the new could not be eaten before the wave sheaf was offered, and both suppose it was left in the barns by inhabitants who had fled into their strong cities. Gill then raises the practical question the reading invites, how Israel got at stored grain while Jericho was shut up so that none went in or out, and offers three answers, that they found it in the outlying villages, or bought it from corn traders, or came upon it in barns outside the walls. Clarke derives the word from a root meaning to pass over and reads it simply as the produce, what passes from the land to the cultivator, or on another authority what passes from hand to hand in trade, so that it means bought corn. Ellicott presses that further and denies it need be last year's at all: it seems to be the produce of that very harvest, brought to the camp probably for sale. Keil takes it as plain corn grown in Canaan.

On why the manna stopped the reasoning is unusually uniform, and the dating is not. Clarke argues from providence, that the supply continued as long as it was needed and ceased when an ordinary provision was at hand, and that its whole history proves it preternatural; Wesley says the same more sharply, that God would not be prodigal of his favours by working miracles where ordinary means suffice. Gill reads the cessation as a type, the manna standing for Christ held forth in the ordinances, which continue until all the spiritual Israel has passed over Jordan and then cease. On the day itself they part. Wesley puts it on the seventeenth, and Clarke on the same day, quoting an authority who reasons that the sheaf was offered on the sixteenth in broad daylight while the manna fell only at night. Ellicott makes it the sixteenth, and builds on that date the observation that gives this entry its most striking claim: reckoning from its first appearance he finds it fell thirty-nine years and eleven months, always resting on the Sabbath, and ceased at last on the day of the week later marked by the resurrection, so that the risen Christ takes the place of the bread from heaven.
13:
Where Joshua was standing gets more attention than the phrase seems to warrant, because the Hebrew says in Jericho. Gill takes it for the border or the side of the city rather than the city itself, and reads him as reconnoitring alone, looking for a place to attack or an easier way in, and very likely praying for direction. He reports that Ben Gersom read the phrase as meaning his thoughts were in Jericho, and that both he and Abarbinel made the whole thing a prophetic vision or night dream, which Gill rejects: whether by day or night, it was a real sight. Wesley settles it as the adjoining territory. Henry keeps both possibilities, praying or surveying the fortifications, and draws his own note from the second, that God helps those who help themselves, and that Joshua was in his post as a general when God made himself known as Generalissimo. Calvin fastens on the words about lifting his eyes, taking them as a guard against the suspicion that his sight had been dazzled by some evanescent phantom, and adds that the vision was not given for Joshua's private benefit but to confirm the whole people and furnish posterity with proof.

On who the man was they are unusually agreed, and the agreement is argued rather than assumed. Clarke, Wesley, Henry and Calvin all take him for the Son of God, and give the same three grounds: he accepted worship that a created angel would have refused, as the angel in the Revelation refused it; the ground was made holy by his presence, which is God's prerogative; and he is called Jehovah in the following chapter. Wesley states the three most compactly, Clarke adds that Joshua was not reprehended for offering divine worship, and Henry notes that to Abraham in his tent he had appeared as a traveller and here in the field as a man of war, since Christ will be to his people what their faith expects. Calvin argues the case against opponents by name. He rejects the view of Grotius and other moderns that this was a created angel, and traces it to the Rabbis, who went further and fixed on Michael with nothing stronger than a verse in Daniel to support them. He is equally careful on the other side: Christ did not then become incarnate, and what appeared was a likeness of man, whether substantial body or outward form being needless to discuss.

Ellicott presses the answer harder than the others. The captain replies neither for us nor for them, which means that Jehovah takes part in this conflict not as an ally and not as an adversary but as commander-in-chief; it is not Israel's quarrel in which divine assistance is sought, but the Lord's own quarrel, in which Joshua and Israel are only a division of his host. Ellicott thinks the distinction worth remembering because the conquest is too often described as an Israelite enterprise for which divine sanction was afterwards claimed. He also sets the appearance against the bush at Horeb, where the same command about the shoe was given: the bush burning and not consumed showed suffering Israel in the furnace, with God afflicted in their affliction, whereas the drawn sword is the sign of victory, God no longer suffering with his people but standing forth to lead them. Henry reads the same sword as authorization, since when the sovereign draws it war is proclaimed and the subject may draw too. Calvin answers the difficulty of a captain saying he has now come when he had never left, that God is said to come when his help is actually felt, and takes the loosened shoe as a concession to human weakness rather than a value in itself.
